USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Implement the already-noticed List 3 tariffs at the original 10 percent rate on about $200 billion of Chinese goods, keep the $50 billion Section 301 duties in place, and do not raise List 3 to 25 percent now. Pair that with a public invitation to resume talks on the Section 301 structural issues—IP theft, forced tech transfer, and industrial targeting—not another purchase MOU. Use the just-completed hearing record to grant targeted exclusions where US firms have no realistic non-China input, so the next step is pressure, not a self-inflicted consumer shock.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat reading is modestly elevated, not existential. The US macro is still absorbing the fight: Michigan sentiment is 100.1, industrial production is up, and VIX is about 14. The damage is concentrated, not systemic. US goods exports to China have already fallen (about $10.5B in April to $9.3B in August), China matched the $50B package on soybeans, autos, and aircraft, and November beans were about 17 percent below pre-retaliation levels, forcing a $12B farm-aid program with soybeans taking ~$3.6B of the first tranche. That is a real hit to a politically and commercially exposed export sector, and List 3 would start taxing consumer and intermediate goods (bikes, furniture, appliances) that US firms told USTR they cannot quickly reshore. Those costs keep the score above zero. It is not +0.5 because there is still no material GDP drag, credit stress, or market panic, and the dollar is strong.

The action is escalate_tariffs because the May joint statement already showed the alternative: China offered larger purchases, Mnuchin called the war “on hold,” and the White House had to collapse the truce on May 29 to keep Section 301 alive. Mid-level talks on August 22–23 produced no structural movement and no follow-on date. China has already retaliated dollar-for-dollar on the $50B lists, so failing to follow through on the June 18 / July 10 List 3 contingency would treat that threat as a bluff. A 10 percent List 3 rate preserves leverage while China still has more bilateral surplus to lose than the US has remaining goods for Beijing to tax (~$130–135B of US goods vs a $200B US list). Raising the rate to 25 percent now, or adding another $200B immediately, would push costs onto US households just as harvest and midterms arrive, and would invite the non-tariff tools China has already signaled once it runs out of US goods. CNY has already weakened about 8 percent since spring (DEXCHUS ~6.33 to ~6.83), which blunts some of the tariff bite and argues against piling on rate hikes before the 10 percent list is even in force.
key_factors: Section 301 $50B package fully in force and China has matched it
List 3 $200B comment/hearing process is complete; 10% vs 25% is the live choice
US farm exports, especially soybeans, are the main bilateral pain point
US macro still strong; China FX and slower IP show more strain than US GDP
August 22-23 talks failed on structural issues; May purchase-only truce already collapsed
Yuan depreciation and import front-loading are blunting US tariff leverage

sources_cited.excerpt: USTR Section 301 report finds China's IP/tech-transfer practices unreasonable; Trump directs tariffs, a WTO case, and investment restrictions.
Joint statement: China agrees to significantly increase purchases; Mnuchin says trade war is on hold.
White House announces the US will proceed with Section 301 25% tariffs on ~$50B; truce collapses.
List 1 takes effect: US 25% on ~$34B; China imposes matching ~$34B the same day.
USTR publishes proposed List 3: ~$200B of Chinese imports for an additional 10% tariff.
At Trump's direction, USTR says it is considering raising the proposed List 3 rate from 10% to 25%.
List 2 takes effect: US 25% on ~$16B, completing the $50B package; China matches ~$16B.
US goods exports to China fell from $10.51B (Apr) to $9.28B (Aug); latest $9.73B (Sep).
US goods imports from China rose from $38.2B (Apr) to $49.9B (Sep), consistent with front-loading ahead of List 3.
CNY weakened from about 6.33 in mid-March to 6.827 on 2018-09-05 (~8%), offsetting part of the tariff.
Michigan consumer sentiment 100.1 in September; US demand not cracking.
VIX 13.91 on 2018-09-05; no financial-stress signal from the dispute.
Aug 22-23 Malpass-Wang talks ended with no breakthrough and no further talks scheduled; US pressed structural 301 issues, not purchases.
USDA: up to $12B authorized; initial MFP ~$4.7B with soybeans $1.65/bu (~$3.63B), plus $1.2B purchases.
November soybeans ~$8.45, down ~17% since China's April duty announcement; China takes roughly one-third of US soybean rows.
Nearly 400 firms testified that List 3 would raise prices on bikes, car seats, appliances and force job cuts because US capacity is gone.
China bought only ~$135B of US goods last year, so it cannot match $200B in tariffs and is more likely to use non-tariff tools.
